concepts.name: Dhar Commission (1948): Mandate, Findings and Rejection of Linguistic Basis
key_dimensions: S.K. Dhar Commission's primary mandate — administrative efficiency over linguistic reorganisation
Key recommendation: administrative convenience should override language as the basis for state formation
Why UPSC sets traps: often confused with JVP Committee; both rejected linguistic basis initially but for different reasons
Historical significance: first formal inquiry post-independence that set the stage for later reversal

concepts.name: JVP Committee (1949): Composition, Report and Conditional Rejection
key_dimensions: Composition: Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya — the political weight behind the committee
Nuanced position: rejected immediate linguistic reorganisation but left a conditional door open ('if sentiments are too strong')
Distinction from Dhar Commission: JVP was a political committee vs. Dhar's administrative/legal character
UPSC trap: JVP did NOT completely reject linguistic basis — it deferred it, a critical distinction

concepts.name: Potti Sriramulu Fast and the Formation of Andhra State (1952–53)
key_dimensions: Potti Sriramulu's 58-day fast-unto-death and its political consequences on Nehru's government
Andhra State carved out of Madras State in October 1953 — first state formed on linguistic basis
Trigger effect: created a domino demand for linguistic states across India
UPSC trap: Andhra State (1953) is distinct from Andhra Pradesh (1956); the latter included Telangana after States Reorganisation Act

concepts.name: Fazl Ali Commission (States Reorganisation Commission, 1953–55): Mandate and Composition
key_dimensions: Three-member composition: Fazl Ali (Chairman), H.N. Kunzru, K.M. Panikkar — their backgrounds and significance
Mandate: comprehensive review of the entire question of reorganisation, not just linguistic states
Four factors framework: language, geography, economic viability, and administrative convenience
UPSC trap: SRC was NOT constituted solely for linguistic reorganisation — it had a broader multi-factor mandate

concepts.name: Four-Factor Framework of the Fazl Ali Commission: Language vs. Other Criteria
key_dimensions: The four criteria: (1) preservation of India's unity and security, (2) linguistic and cultural homogeneity, (3) financial, economic, and administrative considerations, (4) planning and promotion of welfare
Language accepted as an important but NOT the sole criterion — nuanced position often misquoted
Rejection of 'one language–one state' formula: acknowledged multilingual realities
UPSC trap: the SRC explicitly rejected making language the ONLY basis, yet the Act is popularly called 'linguistic reorganisation'

concepts.name: States Reorganisation Act 1956: Key Constitutional Amendments Enabling It
key_dimensions: 7th Constitutional Amendment Act 1956: abolished Part A, B, C, D state distinctions; created only States and Union Territories
Article 3 and Article 4: Parliament's power to form new states, alter boundaries, change names — ordinary legislation sufficiency
UPSC trap: reorganisation under Article 3 does NOT require consent of the concerned state legislature — only consultation
Relationship between 7th Amendment and States Reorganisation Act: they operated simultaneously on November 1, 1956

concepts.name: Abolition of the Four-Part Classification of States (Parts A, B, C, D)
key_dimensions: Pre-1956 classification: Part A (former Governor's provinces), Part B (former princely states), Part C (centrally administered), Part D (Andaman & Nicobar)
Post-1956 binary: States and Union Territories — significance for federal structure
UPSC trap: Hyderabad, Mysore, Travancore-Cochin were Part B states — their merger/reorganisation was politically sensitive
Rajpramukh abolition: Part B states had Rajpramukhs (ex-rulers) replaced by Governors — democratic uniformity achieved

concepts.name: Formation of New States Under SRA 1956: State-wise Analysis of Mergers and Bifurcations
key_dimensions: Andhra Pradesh: merger of Andhra State + Telangana (from Hyderabad) — contested merger with Gentlemen's Agreement 1956
Kerala: merger of Travancore-Cochin + Malabar district from Madras — Malayalam-speaking unification
Karnataka (then Mysore): merger of Mysore, Coorg, parts of Bombay, Hyderabad, Madras — Kannada consolidation
UPSC trap: Bombay and Punjab were NOT reorganised purely on linguistic lines in 1956 — their bifurcation came later (1960 and 1966 respectively)

concepts.name: Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960: Maharashtra–Gujarat Bifurcation and Samyukta Maharashtra/Mahagujarat Movements
key_dimensions: SRC 1956 had recommended a bilingual Bombay state — rejected by both Marathi and Gujarati communities
Samyukta Maharashtra Movement (Marathi) and Mahagujarat Movement (Gujarati): parallel linguistic agitations
Bombay city dispute: initially proposed as a separate centrally-administered territory — political compromise eventually gave it to Maharashtra
UPSC trap: Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 was a POST-SRA event, showing SRA was NOT the final word on reorganisation

concepts.name: Punjab Reorganisation Act 1966: Punjabi Suba and Religious vs. Linguistic Basis
key_dimensions: Akali Dal demand for Punjabi Suba: officially framed as linguistic (Punjabi language) but perceived as having religious (Sikh majority) underpinning
Shah Commission 1966: recommended bifurcation into Punjab (Punjabi-speaking) and Haryana (Hindi-speaking)
Chandigarh as Union Territory: shared capital between Punjab and Haryana — a deliberate ambiguity that persists
UPSC trap: SRC 1956 had explicitly REJECTED Punjabi Suba demand — 1966 reorganisation contradicted SRC's recommendation

concepts.name: Nagaland (1963) and North-East Reorganisation: Ethnicity vs. Language as Reorganisation Basis
key_dimensions: Nagaland (1963): first state carved out on ethnic/tribal identity basis, NOT linguistic — a deliberate exception to the linguistic principle
Meghalaya (1972), Manipur, Tripura: further recognition of ethnic/tribal distinctiveness over linguistic homogeneity
North-East Reorganisation significance: demonstrated that the linguistic principle was a dominant but NOT universal rule
UPSC trap: the linguistic principle established in 1956 had built-in exceptions from the very beginning — North-East is the primary evidence

concepts.name: Gentlemen's Agreement 1956: Andhra Pradesh Formation and Telangana Safeguards
key_dimensions: Agreement between Andhra leaders and Telangana leaders to protect Telangana's interests in the merged state
Key provisions: regional committee for Telangana, proportional representation in services and education (mulki rules)
Mulki Rules controversy: led to Jai Telangana movement (1969) and ultimately Telangana state in 2014
UPSC trap: Gentlemen's Agreement was NOT a constitutional provision — it was a political understanding, hence easily violated

concepts.name: Role of Article 3 in Post-1956 Reorganisations: Parliament's Plenary Power
key_dimensions: Article 3 allows Parliament to: form new states, increase/diminish area, alter boundaries, change names
State legislature's role: only consultation required, NOT concurrence — Parliament can override state opinion
Babulal Parate case (1960): Supreme Court upheld Parliament's plenary power under Article 3 without requiring state consent
UPSC trap: Article 3 reorganisation is by ordinary legislation (simple majority) — NOT a constitutional amendment requiring special majority

concepts.name: Linguistic Minorities and the States Reorganisation Act: Safeguards and Failures
key_dimensions: Creation of linguistic states simultaneously created linguistic minorities within those states (e.g., Kannada speakers in Maharashtra, Marathi speakers in Karnataka)
Article 347 and Article 350A: provisions for linguistic minorities — instruction in mother tongue at primary level
Belgaum (Belagavi) dispute: Marathi-speaking pockets in Karnataka, unresolved since 1956 — tested by Mahajan Commission 1966
UPSC trap: SRC 1956 created the linguistic minority problem even as it solved the linguistic majority demand — a paradox

concepts.name: Mahajan Commission 1966: Maharashtra–Karnataka Border Dispute and Its Non-Implementation
key_dimensions: Constituted to resolve the Belgaum/Belagavi and border disputes between Maharashtra and Karnataka post-1956
Recommendation: awarded majority of disputed areas to Karnataka; Maharashtra rejected the findings
Non-implementation status: Mahajan Commission report was never formally implemented — dispute remains live
UPSC trap: Mahajan Commission is often confused with Shah Commission (Punjab); both were 1966 but dealt with entirely different issues

concepts.name: Demands for New States Post-SRA: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand (2000) — Tribal/Regional vs. Linguistic Basis
key_dimensions: All three states formed in 2000 were based on regional/tribal/developmental identity — NOT linguistic basis
Jharkhand: tribal identity and exploitation narrative; Chhattisgarh: regional development argument; Uttarakhand: hill-plains divide
Evolution of reorganisation criteria: from linguistic (1956) to multi-dimensional identity and governance efficiency (2000)
UPSC trap: these states demonstrate that the 'linguistic basis' of reorganisation was progressively diluted — later reorganisations followed different logic

concepts.name: Telangana State (2014): Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act and the Consent Controversy
key_dimensions: Andhra Pradesh legislature passed a NEGATIVE resolution against bifurcation — Parliament ignored it using Article 3 powers
Telangana: based on historical, cultural, and economic sub-regional identity within a linguistically homogeneous Telugu-speaking state
Significance: first post-independence case of bifurcating a linguistically homogeneous state — reversed the 1956 logic
UPSC trap: the creation of Telangana directly contradicted the premise of the 1956 merger — unity of Telugu speakers was the justification for AP in 1956

concepts.name: Sarkaria Commission (1983–87) and Inter-State Council on Reorganisation Demands: Centre–State Dimension
key_dimensions: Sarkaria Commission: examined Centre-State relations including the process of state formation and reorganisation
Recommendation: a permanent Inter-State Council under Article 263 for dispute resolution including boundary disputes
Inter-State Council established 1990 (not 1983): UPSC trap on the time gap between recommendation and implementation
Relevance to reorganisation: Sarkaria highlighted that ad hoc reorganisation creates long-term federal tensions — systemic mechanism needed

concepts.name: National Integration vs. Linguistic Reorganisation: Nehru's Evolving Position
key_dimensions: Nehru's 1928 support for linguistic provinces (Nehru Report) vs. his post-independence caution after Partition trauma
Nehru's 1953 reversal: Potti Sriramulu's death forced him to concede — demonstrating political compulsion over ideological conviction
The 'unity in diversity' paradox: linguistic reorganisation was argued both as a threat to AND a strengthener of national unity
UPSC trap: Nehru is often portrayed as consistently anti-linguistic reorganisation — his actual position evolved and was ultimately pragmatic, not principled

concepts.name: Coorg (Kodagu) and Merger Decisions: Small Territories and the Viability Criterion
key_dimensions: Coorg was a separate Part C state before 1956 — merged into Mysore (Karnataka) under SRA 1956
Viability criterion: SRC held that very small territories could not be economically or administratively viable as independent states
Coorg example illustrates the tension between local identity assertions and the SRC's administrative efficiency rationale
UPSC trap: Coorg/Kodagu merger is often overlooked but exemplifies how the SRC applied the economic viability criterion to override identity claims
